name: Pedro Páramo
blurb: Juan Rulfo's novel of a son who goes looking for his father in a town of ghosts
title: Pedro Páramo Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: Juan Rulfo's Pedro Páramo explained: who is alive and who is dead in Comala, the main characters, a plot summary in order, the ending and its themes.
h1: Pedro Páramo: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Pedro Páramo is a short novel by the Mexican writer Juan Rulfo, published in 1955 by the Fondo de Cultura Económica. Juan Preciado promises his dying mother that he will go to the town of Comala and find his father, a man named Pedro Páramo, whom he has never met. What he finds there, and the story of Pedro's life told in fragments, make up the book. It is short but hard to follow, because it jumps between times and voices, and it is a core text in Spanish and Latin American schools.

body: Dorotea, a homeless woman of Comala, becomes an important voice in the second half.

The novel is made of dozens of short fragments that move between two lines: Juan Preciado's journey, told by Juan in the first person, and Pedro Páramo's life, told in the third person and out of order. The summary below follows each line in turn.

Juan's journey. Before she dies, Dolores Preciado makes her son promise to go to Comala and demand from his father what he owes them. On the burning road down into the town, Juan meets the mule driver Abundio Martínez, who says that he too is a son of Pedro Páramo and that Pedro died long ago. Comala is empty and silent. Eduviges Dyada takes Juan in, saying his mother told her he was coming, though Dolores is dead; she tells him stories of the past, and later he learns that Eduviges herself killed herself years before. Damiana Cisneros, who cared for him as a baby, leads him through the streets and then vanishes. Juan spends a night with a brother and sister who live together as husband and wife. He hears whispers and voices all around him. Suffocating, he goes out into the street, where the murmurs close in on him, and he dies.

Pedro's rise. As a boy, Pedro flies kites with Susana San Juan and dreams of her; her family later leaves Comala. When his father, Lucas Páramo, is killed at a wedding, Pedro has many of the guests killed in return. He inherits a ruined estate and debts, so with the help of Fulgor Sedano he marries Dolores Preciado to cancel what the family owes her family. Dolores later leaves him with their baby. Pedro takes the land of neighbours who stand in his way and has the surveyor Toribio Aldrete hanged. He fathers many children with many women and takes in only one, Miguel.

Miguel. Miguel Páramo rapes women and kills men, among them the brother of Padre Rentería, and he rapes the priest's niece, Ana. When Miguel's horse throws him and he dies, Pedro gives the priest gold, and Rentería blesses the boy's body against his own conscience. The priest is tormented by having sold his blessings to the powerful.

Susana. Years later Pedro brings Susana and her father, Bartolomé San Juan, back to Comala, and he has Bartolomé killed. Susana, a widow whose husband Florencio has died, has lost her mind; she lives in memories of the sea and of Florencio and never really belongs to Pedro. When revolutionaries come, Pedro buys them off with money and men under his foreman Damasio, called el Tilcuate, and Fulgor Sedano is killed. Later Padre Rentería goes off to join the Cristero rebels.

Susana San Juan dies. The church bells ring for days, people come from all around, and the mourning turns into a fair with music and games. Pedro, enraged, swears that Comala will die of hunger, and he folds his arms and stops working the land. The town empties. Abundio's wife, Refugio, dies, and Abundio, drunk and half deaf, comes to the Media Luna to beg Pedro for money to bury her. He kills Damiana Cisneros when she tries to stop him and stabs Pedro. Pedro, old and alone, sits thinking of Susana, and he collapses into a heap of stones.

The ending turns the first half of the book around. Abundio, who led Juan into Comala at the start, is the one who kills Pedro at the end, so everyone Juan met was already dead. In the middle of the book we learn that Juan is speaking from the grave: he was buried in the same tomb as Dorotea, and their conversation, with the other dead talking in nearby graves, is the frame of the second half. Comala is a town of souls who cannot rest.

The main readings are debated. One reads the novel as a picture of rural Mexico under the cacique, the local strongman: Pedro's greed and violence drain the land of life until only ghosts remain. A second reads it in religious terms, a Catholic purgatory where souls without absolution wait and suffer, with Padre Rentería's failure at its centre. A third, the one Latin American critics usually stress, treats it as an early form of magical realism, where the living and the dead share one world without explanation. Rulfo himself said Pedro's love for Susana was the one clean thing in his life.

ul: Power and the cacique: Pedro owns the land, the courts and even the priest's blessing, and the town lives or dies by his will.
Death and guilt: almost every voice belongs to the dead, and many are trapped by sins they could not confess or have forgiven.
Fathers and abandoned children: Juan, Abundio and Miguel are all Pedro's sons, and none receives what a father should give.
Love that cannot be returned: Pedro gets everything he wants except Susana, and his revenge for her death destroys Comala.
Memory and time: the broken order of the fragments mirrors how the dead keep reliving the past.
Length: a short novel, usually between 120 and 150 pages depending on the edition, divided into short untitled fragments; the first reading is often confusing, and many readers go through it twice.
Background: it is set in rural western Mexico before, during and after the Mexican Revolution and the Cristero War; Rulfo's earlier book was the story collection El Llano en llamas (1953).

Influence and adaptations: Gabriel García Márquez said the novel opened the way for One Hundred Years of Solitude; it has been filmed several times, most recently in 2024 by Rodrigo Prieto. English translations include Margaret Sayers Peden's (1994).
Content: murder, rape, incest and suicide are mentioned, mostly briefly and indirectly.

What teachers usually ask about: the two narrative lines and who is speaking in each fragment, when Juan Preciado died, the meaning of the names Pedro (stone) and Páramo (barren plain), and the novel's place before magical realism.

faq.q: Is Juan Preciado dead in Pedro Páramo?
faq.a: Yes. He dies in Comala after the murmurs of the dead overwhelm him, and in the second half he is speaking from the grave he shares with Dorotea.
Juan Preciado is his son with Dolores; Miguel Páramo is the son he raised; Abundio Martínez is one of many children he had with other women and never acknowledged.
It is usually counted as a forerunner of magical realism, because the living and the dead mix without explanation and because it shaped writers such as García Márquez.
